title: Anahit
author: Ghazaros Aghayan
short_summary: Prince Vachagan, out hunting, meets Anahit at the village spring in Hatsik — the wise daughter of Aran the herdsman. When he sends messengers to ask for her hand, Anahit sets one condition: let him first learn a craft, because fortune changes but a craft never leaves you. Vachagan learns to weave dipak, precious cloth shot with gold thread. Years later, trapped in an underground prison in the city of Peroz, it is that craft that saves his life.
extended_summary:
Prince Vachagan, son of King Vache and Queen Ashkhen, refuses to marry the wealthy bride his parents have chosen and spends his days hunting with his faithful servant Vaghinak and his dog. At the spring in the village of Hatsik, worn out with thirst, he asks for water. A girl named Anahit fills the pitcher and empties it again five or six times before finally letting him drink, and explains why: cold water would harm a man who is hot and sweating, so she delayed on purpose until her guest had cooled down. It is the first time Vachagan has met someone who does not flatter him but thinks about him.

When the messengers come to ask for her hand, Anahit answers: if he wishes me to be his wife, let him first of all learn a craft. Today you are a king and tomorrow you are not, she says, but a craft stays with a person everywhere. Vachagan learns to weave dipak — precious cloth worked with gold and silver thread — and they marry. Years later people begin to disappear from the kingdom, Vaghinak among them. Vachagan follows the trail in disguise, and in the city of Peroz he is tricked underground into the priests' hidden prison, where captives are forced to work. He announces that he is a master weaver, weaves a costly length of cloth, hides his message in the pattern, and insists it be sold only at the palace. Anahit reads the message woven into the pattern, raises troops, tears down the underground prison and frees Vachagan along with every other captive.

questions.prompt: At the spring, Anahit fills the pitcher and empties it five or six times before letting the thirsty Vachagan drink. Why?

options: Cold water would harm a man who is overheated
The pitcher was dirty and needed rinsing out
She did not want to talk to a strange hunter
She wanted the other girls to notice her doing it

questions.explanation: Anahit sees that the man has come from hunting hot and sweating, and she deliberately delays until he has cooled. It is Vachagan's first meeting with someone who does not flatter him but actually looks after him — and the moment he realises who he has met.

questions.prompt: When the messengers come to ask for her hand, Anahit sets one condition: "If he wishes me to be his wife, let him first of all learn a ___."
questions.explanation: Anahit asks for no wealth, no title and no gifts — only a craft. Her argument is simple: today you are a king and tomorrow you are not, but nobody can take a craft out of your hands. The rest of the tale proves her right.

questions.prompt: Which craft does Vachagan learn in order to meet Anahit's condition?

options: Weaving dipak, cloth shot with gold thread
Goldsmithing, making rings and bracelets
Carpentry, making doors and wooden chests
Training horses for the royal stables

questions.explanation: Dipak is a precious cloth woven with gold and silver thread. The choice matters: it is on that cloth that he will later weave the message that saves him. The craft does not only feed him — it gives him a way to speak where speaking is forbidden.

questions.prompt: Put the events of the tale in the order they happen.

items: Out hunting, Vachagan asks for water at the spring in Hatsik
Anahit sets her condition: let him learn a craft first
Vachagan learns to weave dipak, and the wedding takes place
People begin disappearing from the kingdom, Vaghinak among them
Vachagan is taken captive in the underground prison at Peroz
Anahit brings troops, breaks the prison and frees the captives

questions.explanation: The tale falls into two halves, before the wedding and after it. The first is a love story in which a girl sets a condition; the second is an adventure in which that same condition saves the prince's life. Without the first half there would be no second.

questions.prompt: Match each character to their part in the tale.

right: The herdsman of Hatsik, in whose house a wise daughter grows up
The faithful servant who disappears in Peroz
The mother who wanted quite a different bride for her son
The master of the pit, who forces the captives to work

questions.explanation: No character here is spare. The wisdom comes out of a herdsman's house; a servant's disappearance is what puts Vachagan on the road; the mother's resistance shows what it means to choose by the person rather than the birth; and the high priest shows where living off other people's work leads.

questions.prompt: Sort each event by when it happens in the tale.

content.groupA: Before Vachagan and Anahit are married

options.label: A girl empties a pitcher five or six times
Messengers arrive to ask for a girl's hand
A prince sits down at a weaver's loom
Vaghinak is sent away and never comes back
A traveller in disguise is tricked at Peroz
A costly patterned cloth reaches the palace

questions.explanation: The point of the tale lies exactly in the join between its two halves: what looked in the first like a girl's strange whim — learn a craft first — becomes in the second a matter of life and death.

questions.prompt: In the underground prison Vachagan announces that he is a master weaver. How does that let him get a message out?

options: He weaves the message into the pattern and demands it be sold at the palace
He trades the cloth to a guard in exchange for his freedom
He hides a letter inside the cloth and throws it over the wall
He sends an apprentice to the palace, as a master is entitled to

questions.explanation: The captives are not allowed to speak, but nobody suspects a pattern in a piece of cloth. Vachagan weaves into it where he is and what is happening, and insists that a buyer for anything so costly will only be found at the palace. The craft gives him a voice in a place with no voices.

questions.prompt: Anahit knew Vachagan was a prince who would never need to work. Why then did she insist on a craft?

options: Because fortune changes, but a craft stays with a person
Because she wanted to test how patient he could be
Because in the village nobody could marry without one
Because her father demanded it as the price of a bride

questions.explanation: Anahit's argument is that rank and riches can vanish overnight, while skill in your hands cannot. The tale then proves it literally: the title of prince was worth nothing in the pit, and a weaver's hands saved him and every other captive with him.

questions.prompt: Anahit refused the prince until he had learned a craft. Was she right to do that, or was it too hard a condition to put on someone who loved her? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both positions can earn full marks. A strong 'yes' answer remembers that the ending proves her right — the craft saved not only her husband but every captive in the pit. A strong 'no' answer might argue that love is not measured in conditions, or that they could have married first and learned the craft afterwards. Accept any answer that supports its position with events from the tale.

questions.prompt: Imagine Anahit set you the same condition: learn something that would keep you anywhere. What would you choose to learn today, and how might it help you out of a difficult spot?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer names one specific skill and explains how exactly it would help in trouble — not 'it is a good job' but 'here is what I would do with it'. Any skill with a practical explanation earns full marks.

questions.prompt: Anahit lived in the village of ___, where Vachagan met her at the spring.
questions.explanation: Hatsik is an ordinary village, not a capital or a fortress. The tale deliberately puts its wisdom in a herdsman's house rather than in a palace: even the village elders come to Anahit for advice.

questions.prompt: When Anahit reads the message woven into the pattern of the cloth, what does she do?

options: Raises troops, breaks open the prison and frees every captive
Sends a ransom to the priests to buy her husband back
Waits for the king, her husband's father, to decide
Puts on a disguise and goes to Peroz to search herself

questions.explanation: Anahit neither waits nor pays. She acts at once, and saves not only her husband but everyone who had vanished. The girl who gave wise advice at the beginning of the tale is, by the end, the one who makes the decision and carries it out.
